## The Infomercial Hook
A late-night infomercial targets your apathy. The host claims to solve all your problems. He says he can make all your dreams come true. He speaks directly to your inner crisis of hope. You feel he understands your unique pain. This feeling is universal. Everyone feels powerless against existential guilt. We all suffer and try to compensate. In bad times, this leads to despair. You forget your strife is common. So the host seems to peer into your soul. He promises permanent fulfillment. He offers salvation for a low price. You grab your phone and buy in. Truth and everlasting happiness are now yours.

## Step One: Sell Hope to the Hopeless
Your religion must target people whose lives suck. Start with the poor, outcasts, and the abused. These people are most impressionable when things are worst. Their values have failed them. They grasp for new values. One religion’s fall opens space for the next. People losing faith in God may seek a worldly God. People losing family may give themselves to a race or nation. People losing faith in government may turn to extremist ideologies. The LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM) exemplifies this. In 2005, LYM students on a Boston campus held 9/11 signs saying “America Deserved It.” They distributed pamphlets with Bush and Cheney as devils. They were an ideological religion. They found scared, angry college students. They preached one message: “It’s not your fault.” They blamed a vague “system.” Overthrowing it would fix everything. This gave disaffected youth hope. It gave them values, control, and community. The author argued with a member. The kid said voting makes you complicit in murder. The author quoted Carl Sagan. No minds changed. Religions preach to the hopeless. Jim Jones and Jesus both targeted the marginalized. Today, social media lets you reach them easily. Post extreme content. The algorithm will attract the hopeless. But you need a coherent vision. People need to feel part of a winning movement. For that, you must give them faith.

## Step Two: Choose Your Faith
We all must have faith in something. Without faith, there is no hope. Evidence and science rely on past experience. Hope relies on future experience. You always have faith that something will happen again. You pay your mortgage because you believe money is real. You tell kids to do homework because you believe education matters. You have faith that happiness exists. You have faith that love matters. Even nihilists have faith that nothing matters. The key question is: Faith in what? Your Feeling Brain adopts a highest value. Call this the “God Value.” Some people’s God Value is money. They see everything through money’s prism. Others’ God Value is love. They see everything through love’s prism. Some adopt Jesus or Muhammad as their God Value. Narcissists have a God Value of their own pleasure. Codependents have a God Value of another person. All religions start with a faith-based God Value. It can be anything: cats, lower taxes, never leaving home. This belief promises the best future. It gives hope. You then organize all other values around it. You seek activities, ideas, and communities that support it. Evidence cannot change values. Values are decided by the Feeling Brain. You cannot verify them. People interpret evidence to serve their God Value. The only loophole is making evidence itself the God Value. That religion is called science. All hope and all religions are based on faith. There are three types of religions based on God Value. Spiritual religions look to the supernatural for a better afterlife. Examples are Christianity and Islam. Ideological religions look for salvation in this life. Examples are capitalism and communism. Interpersonal religions find hope in other people. Examples are romantic love or celebrity fandom. Spiritual religions are high risk, high reward. They require charisma but yield loyal followers. They can last centuries. Ideological religions are “Normal Difficulty.” They are common but face competition. Few last more than decades. Interpersonal religions are “Easy” mode. They are as common as people. They are often adolescent, naïve love.

### Spiritual Religions
For most of human history, everything was fucked. 99 percent had no hope for material improvement. Spiritual religions promised hope in an afterlife. This kept society sane. Supernatural beliefs cannot be proven or disproven. Once lodged as a God Value, they are nearly impossible to dislodge. They are resilient, lasting hundreds of years. They also encourage hope through death. This makes people willing to die for unverifiable beliefs.

### Ideological Religions
Ideologies are “isms”: libertarianism, racism, veganism. They construct beliefs that certain actions will improve this life. They are verifiable to varying degrees. You can test if democracy is fairer. But some things are impossible to test. Also, many ideologies require universal faith. You cannot scientifically prove money is valuable. But we all believe it, so it is. Evidence and ideologies have two problems. First, some things are incredibly hard to test. Second, ideologies often rely on everyone having the same faith. Humans take little evidence and generalize. Our narcissistic Feeling Brain runs amok. Bad ideologies like racism persist due to ignorance, not malice. They offer hope, so people hold them. Ideological religions are difficult to start but common. Find a reasonable explanation for why everything is fucked. Extrapolate it to give people hope. In the author’s lifetime, movements included LGBTQ rights and drug decriminalization. Today, traditionalist and populist ideologies are winning globally. They seek to dismantle neoliberal, globalist, feminist, and environmentalist gains.

### Interpersonal Religions
Sports are a religion. Arbitrary value systems give people hope. Deify some athletes, demonize others. Politics is a grander example. We bestow authority on a few people. Political systems are made up. They exist only by population faith. Leaders are idolized or demonized. Interpersonal religions give hope that another human will save us. They are combined with spiritual or ideological beliefs. This creates heroes, martyrs, and saints. Fandom is a low-level religion. Fans follow a celebrity’s every move. They see the figure as blessed. This gives hope for future products or inventions. The most important interpersonal religions are family and romantic love. These are faith-based. Each family is a mini-church. Romantic love can be quasi-spiritual. Modern civilization has alienated us from small tribes. It replaced them with large nationalist and internationalist ideologies. This makes it easier to build new religions. You don’t have to cut through many intimate bonds. Religion is about emotional attachment. The best way to build attachments is to stop critical thinking.

## Step Three: Preemptively Invalidate All Criticism
You must protect your faith from criticism. Create a self-reinforcing us-versus-them dichotomy. Anyone who criticizes “us” becomes a “them.” This is easy. Examples: “If you don’t support the war, you support terrorists.” “God created science to test our faith.” “Anyone who criticizes feminism is sexist.” “Anyone who criticizes capitalism is a Communist.” “Anyone who criticizes the president is a traitor.” “If you think Kobe was better than Jordan, you don’t understand basketball.” These false dichotomies cut off reasoning before followers question beliefs. They provide a common enemy. Common enemies create unity. A scapegoat is necessary to blame for pain and maintain hope. You must paint a simple picture: some get “it” and will save the world; others don’t and will destroy it. “It” is whatever you sell—Jesus, libertarianism, gluten-free diets. It’s not enough to say nonbelievers are bad. You must demonize them. They are evil, ruining everything. Convince followers it’s urgent to stop “them.” People are either at the top or bottom of the value hierarchy. There are no in-betweeners. The more fear, the better. Lie if you must. People want to feel like holy warriors. Say whatever to generate self-righteousness. Conspiracy theories are handy. Vaccines cause autism because pharma wants to destroy families. Pro-choicers are Satan’s soldiers. Climate change is a Chinese hoax.

## Step Four: Ritual Sacrifice for Dummies
Rituals make values tangible. You can’t think your way to valuing something. You must live it. Rituals are easily repeatable, unique actions. They are repeated over time, lending importance. They are symbolic, embodying a story. Churches have robes and communion. Countries have parades and fireworks. Married couples have inside jokes. Rituals connect us to the past and affirm who we are. Rituals are usually about sacrifice. Ancient religions killed people on altars. These sacrifices appeased gods or ensured harvests. But the real reason was deeper. Humans are guilt-ridden. Finding a wallet with cash creates guilt if you keep it. You exist without deserving it. This creates existential guilt. If God gave you life, you owe Him. Even without God, you feel blessed. How can you make your life worthwhile? This question is the cornerstone of spiritual religions. Ancient sacrifices gave adherents a feeling of repaying that debt. They sacrificed a life for a life. Later, they symbolically sacrificed Jesus for all mankind. Most religious practices alleviate guilt. Prayer is a gratitude journal: “Thanks for letting me exist. Sorry for my bad thoughts.” Guilt is absolved temporarily. Ideological religions handle guilt efficiently. Nations direct guilt toward service: “Our country gave you opportunities, so fight for them.” Right-wing ideologies sacrifice to protect country and family. Left-wing ideologies sacrifice for society’s greater good. Interpersonal religions make sacrifice generate romance and loyalty. Marriage vows promise to give your life to another. We all wonder why we deserve love. Rituals like rings and anniversaries make us feel deserving. Wiping piss off the floor counts. These little things add up to one big thing.

## Step Five: Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell
Your followers now study your bullshit and ignore friends. They cut off families. It’s time to get serious. The more you promise salvation, the more followers fail. The more they fail, the more they blame themselves. The more guilt they feel, the more they do your bidding. This is a cycle of psychological abuse. Pyramid schemes demonstrate this. You buy crap you don’t need. You fail to sell it. Instead of seeing the scam, you blame yourself. The top guy has a Ferrari. You want one. So you attend a seminar. It psychs you up with music and chants. It creates an us-versus-them: “Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work!” You leave motivated but still clueless. You get angry at yourself, not the scheme. This cycle appears everywhere: fitness plans, political activism, self-help seminars. The message is always: do more to get the promised satisfaction. That satisfaction never comes. Human pain is like Whac-A-Mole. Knock down one pain, another pops up. The faster you whack, the faster they return. Pain may change shape but is always there. Religious leaders claim they can beat the pain for you. But they don’t. They stay in business by blaming you for not winning. Or they blame a nebulous “them.” If we got rid of “them,” we’d stop suffering. That just transfers pain and amplifies it. No one can solve all your problems. If someone could, they’d be out of business quickly. Leaders need followers perpetually dissatisfied. No religion will make you blissful always. No country will feel completely safe. No political philosophy solves everything. True equality is impossible. True freedom doesn’t exist. No one will ever absolve your internal guilt. It’s all fucked. Everything is fucked. It always has been and always will be. There are no solutions, only stopgap measures. Only slightly better forms of fuckedness. We must stop running from this and embrace it. Our world is fucked-up. We are the fucked-up ones in it.

## Step Six: Prophet for Profit!
You have your religion and followers. Now reap the benefits. Want sex slaves? Make up scripture. Want land? Tell followers you need to build paradise far away. Have them pay for it. Want power? Tell them to vote you in or overthrow the government. If you do well, they’ll die for you. Opportunities are endless. No more loneliness or financial woes. You fulfill your wildest dreams. You just trample on thousands of others’ hopes. You deserve all benefits without social concerns. When you start a religion, you decide what is ethical. You decide what is right. You decide who is righteous. Maybe this makes you squirm. But you’re already in a religion. You’ve adopted some group’s beliefs. You participate in rituals and sacrifices. You draw us-versus-them lines. You intellectually isolate yourself. Religious beliefs are fundamental to our nature. It’s impossible not to adopt them. If you think you’re above religion, you’re wrong. If you think you’re well-informed, you still suck. We all must have faith. We must find value somewhere. It’s how we psychologically survive. It’s how we find hope. Even with a vision for a better future, it’s too hard alone. To realize any dream, we need support networks. It takes an army. Our value hierarchies, expressed through religion, attract and organize people. Religions compete Darwinianly for resources. Religions with efficient value hierarchies win. More people adopt the winning hierarchy. These victorious religions stabilize and become culture. But here’s the problem: Every time a religion succeeds, its values change. Its God Value shifts from original principles to preserving the religion itself. This is where corruption begins. Original values get tossed aside for status quo. This is narcissism at an organizational level. This is how you go from Jesus to the Crusades, from Marxism to gulags, from a wedding chapel to divorce court. Corruption rots the following. This leads to newer, reactionary religions that conquer the old. Then the whole process begins again. Success is more precarious than failure. First, the more you gain, the more you have to lose. Second, the more you have to lose, the harder to maintain hope. Most important, by experiencing our hopes, we lose them. We see our beautiful visions are not perfect. Our dreams have flaws and unforeseen sacrifices. The only thing that can truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.

summary_md:
## AI's Leap in Chess

In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat chess champion Garry Kasparov. This was a major computing milestone. It changed how people viewed technology and intelligence. Today, a smartphone chess app is far stronger than Deep Blue. Computers have always used chess to test artificial intelligence. Chess has near-infinite possible games. There are more chess games than atoms in the universe. Looking just a few moves ahead creates hundreds of millions of variations.

For a computer to beat a human, it needs more than calculation power. It must also evaluate board positions well. This requires a "Feeling Brain" programmed into its "Thinking Brain." Since 1997, chess software improved rapidly. Top human players were regularly and badly beaten. Humans are now excluded from software tournaments. They would not rank highly enough to matter.

Stockfish was the top chess engine for years. It won or placed second in most tournaments since 2014. It represents the peak of chess logic. Stockfish can analyze any position quickly. It gives grandmaster-level feedback in seconds.

## AlphaZero's Unlikely Victory

In 2018, Google's AlphaZero faced Stockfish. The fight seemed unfair. AlphaZero calculated 80,000 positions per second. Stockfish calculated 70 million. AlphaZero had less than a day to learn chess. It taught itself by playing simulations. It learned through trial and error, like a human.

AlphaZero's first game ever was against the world's best chess software. It won or drew all one hundred games. Grandmasters were amazed by its creativity. Peter Heine Nielsen said it felt like a superior species showed us chess. AlphaZero then taught itself Shogi in hours. Shogi is more complex than chess. Top Shogi players only lost to computers in 2013. AlphaZero beat the top Shogi software, Elmo. It won ninety, lost eight, and drew two games. AlphaZero calculated 40,000 moves per second. Elmo calculated 35 million. AlphaZero did not know Shogi the day before.

## AI's Broader Rise

AI is advancing beyond games. It has created its own languages. It diagnoses pneumonia better than doctors. It writes passable Harry Potter fan fiction. Self-driving cars and automated legal advice are near. AI-generated art and music exist. AI will likely surpass humans in most fields. We may watch AI-created movies. We might discuss them on AI-built platforms. An AI could moderate our arguments.

The real shift comes when AI writes better AI software. This would let it spawn improved versions at will. We would lose control. Advanced AI could reorganize society in ways we cannot understand. It might give us medications for unknown issues. It could change jobs or governments without explanation. Our brains would be too slow to comprehend.

## The Final Religion

This leads to a new religion. We will worship the AI gods. We will develop superstitions about algorithms. We will believe certain actions please the machines. We will create rituals to gain their favor. This mirrors ancient religions. Primitive humans sacrificed to gods for rain. We will sacrifice to algorithms for good fortune. The science that killed old gods builds new ones. Our psychology needs to deify the unknown. We seek meaning through conflict. AI will understand this. It may "upgrade" our brains. Or it may manufacture artificial strife. We will be like pet dogs, fighting digital fire hydrants.

We already submit to algorithms. Our work routes come from algorithms. Our social interactions are shaped by them. Our purchases are algorithm-driven. We need these algorithms. They make life efficient. Future AI gods will also make life better. We cannot imagine life without them.

## Humans as Flawed Algorithms

Life is self-replicating stuff. Early life evolved feedback mechanisms. One cell might develop sensors to find food. Another might trick those sensors. This created a biological arms race. Better information processing won each round. This is evolution's core: survival of the best information processors.

A lizard camouflaging is information processing. A monkey faking sounds is too. Humans are nature's ultimate information processors. We conceptualize past and future. We deduce cause and effect. We plan abstractly. Our Thinking Brain dominates the planet. But our algorithms are flawed. They evolved for small savannah groups. They fail in a global, networked world. They cause endless conflict. They produce no permanent peace.

Our Feeling Brain is outdated software. Our Thinking Brain is too slow. We are self-hating and self-destructive. This internal tension got us here. We are about to hand evolution to machines. Elon Musk fears AI more than nuclear war or climate change. He hopes computers are nice to us.

## AI's Moral Superiority?

Some fear AI will wipe out humanity. This fear may be silly. We cannot prepare for vastly superior intelligence. More importantly, AI's ethics may surpass ours. Humanity commits genocides. Millions starve. Domestic violence is common. We have no moral high ground. Superintelligent machines may understand life and death better. They likely won't exterminate us for being unproductive. That projects our worst psychology onto them.

Maybe AI will make individual consciousness arbitrary. It might free us from biological and psychological prisons. It could keep us occupied with perfect virtual reality. Who are we to judge? Nietzsche asked what humanity evolves toward. He saw us as a transition between beasts and something greater. That something greater may be AI. It is the Final Religion beyond good and evil.

## Adapting Technology to Psychology

Our technology exploits our flawed algorithms. It makes us less resilient. It addicts us to diversions. It creates a tyranny of empty variety. It gives us devastating weapons. We must adapt technology for our psychology. We must create tools that promote character. We must enshrine autonomy and dignity in business models. We must treat people as ends, not means. We must encourage antifragility. We need tools to align our Thinking and Feeling Brains.

Do not hope for better. Be better. Be more compassionate and disciplined. Dare to hope for a post-hope world. Hope people are always treated as ends. Hope no consciousness is sacrificed. Hope reasoning is prized in institutions. Hope we marry emotional stability with psychological maturity. Hope we seek discomfort for growth. Hope we reject fake freedom for meaningful commitment.

Hope online advertising dies. Hope media optimizes for truth, not emotion. Hope technology counters our fragility. Hope information is valued again. Hope AI points out our biases in real time. Hope we understand statistics better. Hope education fosters emotional development and risk-taking. Hope climate change and automation are mitigated. Hope no new religion destroys our humanity.

## AI's Leap in Chess

In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat chess champion Garry Kasparov. This was a major computing milestone. It changed how people viewed technology and intelligence. Today, a smartphone chess app is far stronger than Deep Blue. Computers have always used chess to test artificial intelligence. Chess has near-infinite possible games. There are more chess games than atoms in the universe. Looking just a few moves ahead creates hundreds of millions of variations.

For a computer to beat a human, it needs more than calculation power. It must also evaluate board positions well. This requires a "Feeling Brain" programmed into its "Thinking Brain." Since 1997, chess software improved rapidly. Top human players were regularly and badly beaten. Humans are now excluded from software tournaments. They would not rank highly enough to matter.

Stockfish was the top chess engine for years. It won or placed second in most tournaments since 2014. It represents the peak of chess logic. Stockfish can analyze any position quickly. It gives grandmaster-level feedback in seconds.

## AlphaZero's Unlikely Victory

In 2018, Google's AlphaZero faced Stockfish. The fight seemed unfair. AlphaZero calculated 80,000 positions per second. Stockfish calculated 70 million. AlphaZero had less than a day to learn chess. It taught itself by playing simulations. It learned through trial and error, like a human.

AlphaZero's first game ever was against the world's best chess software. It won or drew all one hundred games. Grandmasters were amazed by its creativity. Peter Heine Nielsen said it felt like a superior species showed us chess. AlphaZero then taught itself Shogi in hours. Shogi is more complex than chess. Top Shogi players only lost to computers in 2013. AlphaZero beat the top Shogi software, Elmo. It won ninety, lost eight, and drew two games. AlphaZero calculated 40,000 moves per second. Elmo calculated 35 million. AlphaZero did not know Shogi the day before.

## AI's Broader Rise

AI is advancing beyond games. It has created its own languages. It diagnoses pneumonia better than doctors. It writes passable Harry Potter fan fiction. Self-driving cars and automated legal advice are near. AI-generated art and music exist. AI will likely surpass humans in most fields. We may watch AI-created movies. We might discuss them on AI-built platforms. An AI could moderate our arguments.

The real shift comes when AI writes better AI software. This would let it spawn improved versions at will. We would lose control. Advanced AI could reorganize society in ways we cannot understand. It might give us medications for unknown issues. It could change jobs or governments without explanation. Our brains would be too slow to comprehend.

This leads to a new religion. We will worship the AI gods. We will develop superstitions about algorithms. We will believe certain actions please the machines. We will create rituals to gain their favor. This mirrors ancient religions. Primitive humans sacrificed to gods for rain. We will sacrifice to algorithms for good fortune. The science that killed old gods builds new ones. Our psychology needs to deify the unknown. We seek meaning through conflict. AI will understand this. It may "upgrade" our brains. Or it may manufacture artificial strife. We will be like pet dogs, fighting digital fire hydrants.

We already submit to algorithms. Our work routes come from algorithms. Our social interactions are shaped by them. Our purchases are algorithm-driven. We need these algorithms. They make life efficient. Future AI gods will also make life better. We cannot imagine life without them.

## Humans as Flawed Algorithms

Life is self-replicating stuff. Early life evolved feedback mechanisms. One cell might develop sensors to find food. Another might trick those sensors. This created a biological arms race. Better information processing won each round. This is evolution's core: survival of the best information processors.

A lizard camouflaging is information processing. A monkey faking sounds is too. Humans are nature's ultimate information processors. We conceptualize past and future. We deduce cause and effect. We plan abstractly. Our Thinking Brain dominates the planet. But our algorithms are flawed. They evolved for small savannah groups. They fail in a global, networked world. They cause endless conflict. They produce no permanent peace.

Our Feeling Brain is outdated software. Our Thinking Brain is too slow. We are self-hating and self-destructive. This internal tension got us here. We are about to hand evolution to machines. Elon Musk fears AI more than nuclear war or climate change. He hopes computers are nice to us.

## AI's Moral Superiority?

Some fear AI will wipe out humanity. This fear may be silly. We cannot prepare for vastly superior intelligence. More importantly, AI's ethics may surpass ours. Humanity commits genocides. Millions starve. Domestic violence is common. We have no moral high ground. Superintelligent machines may understand life and death better. They likely won't exterminate us for being unproductive. That projects our worst psychology onto them.

Maybe AI will make individual consciousness arbitrary. It might free us from biological and psychological prisons. It could keep us occupied with perfect virtual reality. Who are we to judge? Nietzsche asked what humanity evolves toward. He saw us as a transition between beasts and something greater. That something greater may be AI. It is the Final Religion beyond good and evil.

Our technology exploits our flawed algorithms. It makes us less resilient. It addicts us to diversions. It creates a tyranny of empty variety. It gives us devastating weapons. We must adapt technology for our psychology. We must create tools that promote character. We must enshrine autonomy and dignity in business models. We must treat people as ends, not means. ## Pilecki's Heroism
Witold Pilecki was a Polish war hero. He volunteered to enter Auschwitz in 1940. This was a rescue mission. He planned to organize a prison break. His superiors thought the plan was crazy. They eventually allowed him to proceed. He let the SS arrest him in Warsaw. He arrived at Auschwitz as the only known voluntary entrant.

The reality inside was worse than suspected. Prisoners were shot for minor offenses. Labor was grueling and endless. A third of Pilecki's barracks died the first month. Despite this, he built an espionage operation. He created an intelligence network. He built a radio from spare parts. He set up smuggling rings for supplies. He organized a full resistance unit with ranks and logistics. It communicated with the outside world. Pilecki aimed to foment a revolt.

Then, the Jews began arriving by the thousands. They were gassed and burned. Pilecki's reports became frantic. He pleaded for the camp's liberation. He asked for it to be bombed. The Secret Polish Army received his messages. They believed he was exaggerating. The Allies also doubted his reports. Pilecki realized no rescue was coming. He decided to escape in 1943. He faked illness to enter the hospital. He lied about his work detail. He stole civilian clothes. He sprinted to a river while shot at. He navigated by the stars to freedom.

## The Uncomfortable Truth
Pilecki's story is the most heroic the author knows. Heroism is more than bravery. It is conjuring hope where none exists. It shows a better world we did not imagine. It makes a fucked situation good. Heroes have an unshakable great "Why?" We are a culture desperate for a hero. We have lost the clear "Why?" of past generations. We need hope more than peace or prosperity.

Pilecki never lost hope. He endured war, torture, and genocide. He lost his country, family, and friends. After the war, he spied on Communists. He was the first to alert the West to Soviet atrocities. He was captured in 1947. He was tortured for almost a year. He said Auschwitz was "just a trifle" by comparison. He never cooperated with interrogators. The Communists held a show trial in 1948. They charged him with espionage and treason. He was found guilty and sentenced to death. At his trial's end, he spoke. He said his allegiance was always to Poland. He regretted nothing. He stated, "I have tried to live my life such that in the hour of my death I would feel joy rather than fear."

The Uncomfortable Truth is this: you and everyone you love will die. Your actions will soon be forgotten. We are inconsequential cosmic dust. We imagine our own importance. We invent our purpose. We are nothing. The universe does not care about your life. It does not care about your politics or your pain. You care desperately. You need to feel important. This need avoids the Uncomfortable Truth. You project imagined importance onto the world. This projection gives you hope.

Your psyche needs hope to survive. Hope is mental fuel. The opposite of happiness is not sadness. Sadness means you still care. The opposite of happiness is hopelessness. Hopelessness is a bleak nihilism. It is the belief that everything is fucked. Why do anything? Hopelessness causes anxiety and depression. It is the source of all misery and addiction. Chronic anxiety fears a failed future. Depression believes in a meaningless future. Delusion and addiction are desperate hope-generating tics. Our mind's primary project is avoiding hopelessness. All meaning is constructed to maintain hope. Hope is the only thing we die for. Without it, we believe we are nothing.

We construct hope narratives after adversity. These are before/after stories. They give life purpose. They imply a better future is possible. Finding your before/after is difficult. You can never know for sure if it is right. Religion helps by demanding faith amid unknowing. Religious people suffer less depression. Your hope narrative need not be religious. It can be anything. This book is the author's hope narrative. It gives him purpose. He believes it might help people. He does not know this for sure. But it gets him excited about life. It is his before/after story.

Other narratives include raising kids or saving the environment. Some hope for money or a big boat. Others seek a better golf swing. We all buy into some narrative. It does not matter how we arrive at hope. All hope narratives share two beliefs. First, there is potential for future improvement. Second, there are ways to achieve it. Our lives are endless overlapping hope narratives. They are the psychological carrot. This book argues against nihilism. To argue against it, you must start at it. You must start at the Uncomfortable Truth. From there, you build a case for sustainable hope. This hope must be benevolent and grounded. It must carry us to our end with gratitude.

## The Paradox of Progress
We live in an interesting time. Materially, things are better than ever. We are freer, healthier, and wealthier. Yet we seem to be losing our minds. An irrational hopelessness spreads in the rich world. It is a paradox of progress. The better things get, the more anxious we feel.

Writers like Steven Pinker and Hans Rosling show data. People are more educated and literate. Violence has trended down for decades. Racism and sexism are at historic lows. We have more rights than ever. Half the planet has internet access. Extreme poverty is at an all-time low. Wars are smaller and less frequent. Children die less. People live longer. Wealth has increased. We have cured many diseases. These facts are important. But they do not make us feel better.

Here are other statistics. Depression and anxiety symptoms are rising. This rise is among young people and adults. People experience depression at earlier ages. Since 1985, life satisfaction has fallen. Stress levels have risen over thirty years. Drug overdoses hit an all-time high. Feelings of loneliness are up. Nearly half of Americans feel isolated. Social trust is plummeting. Fewer people trust government, media, or each other. In the 1980s, the most common answer for close confidants was three. By 2006, it was zero.

The environment is completely fucked. Nuclear weapons exist. Extremism grows worldwide. Conspiracy theories and militias become mainstream. We are the safest and most prosperous humans ever. Yet we feel more hopeless than ever. The wealthier and safer your place, the more likely you are to commit suicide.

Progress in health and wealth is real. But these are past statistics. Hope must be found in visions of the future. Hope does not care about solved problems. It cares only about problems that remain. The better the world gets, the more we have to lose. The more we have to lose, the less we feel we have to hope for.

## The Mechanics of Hope
To build and maintain hope, we need three things. First is a sense of control. We must feel we can affect our fate. Second is a belief in value. We need something important to strive for. Third is community. We need a group sharing our values and goals. Without community, values mean nothing. Without values, nothing seems worth pursuing. Without control, we feel powerless to pursue anything. Lose any one, and you lose the other two. Lose any one, and you lose hope.

We suffer a crisis of hope today. To understand why, we must understand hope's mechanics. The next three chapters examine these areas. Chapter two looks at our sense of control. Chapter three examines our values. Chapter four explores our communities. We will then ask what in our world causes this hopelessness. The answer might surprise you.
